prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realization at the 10^-18 level of accuracy, opening new tests of time, gravity and fundamental constants

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part, B013, to Katori and Ye. Having read all eight statements and the chair's questions, I find the unanimity less comforting than it looks, so I tried to break the case rather than count heads. What survives is this. The magic-wavelength lattice is a concrete idea with a concrete physical consequence: the light shift cancels in the clock transition while thousands of atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime. That is what separates it from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. The comb made optical frequencies countable, and the ion work showed control of one quantum system; neither gave many-atom interrogation at 1e-18 stability. Nature has answered: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift has been resolved, and independent laboratories now compare clocks and agree. These are the clues from nature I look for. I accept that a clock does not change our picture of the universe the way a black-hole image might, but a clock that resolves the curvature of time across a millimetre is, to my taste, quite existential enough. Maturity is not in question after more than twenty years of reproduction.
statement.case_against: The honest objection remains distinctness. Precision metrology has been honoured in 1989, 1997, 2001, 2005 and 2012, and a sceptic can call this the next increment on a recognised line. I answer that with the mechanism and the many-atom regime, but I do not pretend the answer is a proof. Two further weaknesses. First, a two-name credit omits Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Derevianko, Oates, Bloom and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, and I cannot verify early strontium and ytterbium priority dates from the material in front of me. Second, my own taste runs toward the Event Horizon Telescope and moire matter. I accept that I cannot yet build a credit for the former that survives Pearce's point about Zensus, nor a maturity case for the latter given the unsettled pairing mechanism, so these remain alternatives and not my configuration.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Katori and Ye are credited for the same achievement or for two separable contributions, and says the prize should reward the original work rather than a second group that did it much better.
responses.response: I think this is the sharpest question for the citation, and I answer it as follows. They are two steps of one achievement, and the citation should say so by naming both. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice demonstration are the invention. Ye's group is not a refinement of a finished idea: the record accuracy, the stability from many atoms and the many-body clock turned a promising scheme into an instrument that others could verify. Without the second step the first would have remained a proposal. For that reason I have rewritten my citation as the invention of the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realization at the 10^-18 level, so that the invention is credited first and the accuracy second, which should meet your concern about rewarding the original work. If other members feel Ye's contribution is performance alone, I would like to hear it now, since that would change my view of the pair.

responses.point: Mehlig asks me to correct my reading of the 2005 prize: it went to Glauber, Hall and Hansch, Ye was Hall's collaborator and not a laureate, so he should not be counted as a prior laureate.
responses.response: I agree, and Kroll made the same correction to me. I raised this in round 1 and it matters because the chair's summary lists six members as saying Ye already shared the 2005 prize. That is a factual slip repeated across several files, and I want it removed from the discussion before the vote. Ye is not a prior laureate. The remaining question is only whether being Hall's collaborator makes the pairing look like the same laboratory family, and I do not think so: the lattice clock was developed in his own group at JILA years after the comb work. I also take your point on the Higgs and agree that any three names from ATLAS and CMS are an arbitrary selection from thousands of colleagues. My preference for the clock rests substantially on the fact that we can write its citation without making that choice.

responses.point: Pearce argues that broad support may reflect clear attribution as much as scientific weight, that the Higgs has arguably greater weight, and that Zensus cannot be omitted from an Event Horizon Telescope credit.
responses.response: I accept both halves of this. On weight, you are right that clean attribution is not the same thing as scientific importance, and I have tried not to let it stand in for importance. My test is whether the result is confirmed by nature and opens something new, and the lattice clock passes it, though I concede that the Higgs discovery is the larger discovery. I would only add that a prize which cannot name its laureates without arbitrary choices does not help the discovery. On B016, your Zensus point is decisive for me, because I had been uneasy about a two-name or three-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds, and a credit that omits the person who built the European mm-VLBI capability is contestable. I also still want more polarization and dynamics results before backing the black-hole images. I therefore keep B016 only as an alternative and do not raise it to a second prize part.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second, and whether the largest payoff of the lattice clock is still to come.
responses.response: My support does not depend on the redefinition, and I would not wait for it. The redefinition of the second is a metrological decision, taken by a different body for different reasons, and it could be delayed for years without changing the science. What we reward is the demonstrated capability: 1e-18 uncertainty, reproduced by independent laboratories, and used to resolve redshifts over millimetres. Waiting would also invite the problem that the committee often meets, in which each year the credit becomes harder to assign as more groups join. I would rather decide now, while the invention and the realization are still clearly attributable to two people.

responses.point: Lindroth states plainly that Katori's proposal and early demonstrations of 2001-2003 and Ye's record-setting realization are the two decisive steps, and that other groups' contributions are real but secondary.
responses.response: I find this a helpful statement of priority from someone close to atomic structure, and it fits my reading. I would qualify one word, as Kroll did: Lemonde's early work and the Sr and Yb comparisons at SYRTE, PTB and NIST were what made the 1e-18 claims credible, since an accuracy figure counts only after independent clocks agree. I would not call that secondary in importance, but I accept it is secondary for the purpose of the credit under a three-person limit. A citation phrased around invention and realization limits the exclusion without naming people who cannot all be named. I also note your declared proximity to the field and think the committee should check your priority dates against the record, which I cannot do myself.

uncertainties: Whether a lattice-clock prize is judged to be distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I think it is, but this is a judgement and I cannot prove it.
Early strontium and ytterbium lattice-clock priority dates and the relative roles of Katori and Ye, and Lemonde's role in particular. I rely on colleagues in atomic physics for these.
Whether the committee will correct the repeated statement that Ye shared the 2005 prize, since six round-1 files relied on it.
Whether the committee wants a second part. I do not see a partner for B013 with a clean attribution within the three-person limit, since only one name would remain.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has appeared in round 1 or in the other members' statements. None of the credited names for B013 is a mentor, collaborator or co-author of mine, and the research I do (string theory, de Sitter space, dark bubble cosmology) is far from precision atomic physics. I note my taste for the Event Horizon Telescope, which is close to my interest in black holes, but it is an alternative only and I have no personal tie to its credited names. I also note that I am listed as a co-opted member and Secretary, which is a procedural matter rather than a conflict.
